Stage 01

Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO transparency, Apostille authentication chain, official name clearance restricted wordlist, and pre-incorporation statutory fee budget.

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Law 10/2010 of 28 April on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, as amended; Royal Decree 304/2014 of 5 May approving its implementing regulation; Royal Decree 609/2023 of 11 July establishing the Central Register of Beneficial Ownership; Royal Decree-law 7/2021 of 27 April implementing, among other matters, EU AML requirements; Law 18/2022 of 28 September on the creation and growth of companies, relevant to simplified incorporation and the minimum capital framework; Spanish Commercial Code and Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 of 2 July approving the Capital Companies Law.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

A Spanish S.L. must have a registered office in Spain, and the office must correspond to the company's effective administrative or principal establishment as required by the Capital Companies Law. A serviced or virtual office may be acceptable where it provides a genuine legally usable address, reliable receipt and forwarding of official notices, access for corporate records, and evidence of actual management activity. A mailbox-only arrangement is inadequate. For a no-code website builder, there is no sector-specific premises license on the stated facts, but the company should maintain demonstrable Spanish management, accounting, contractual, customer-support, data-protection, and banking records. VAT, consumer, digital-services, intellectual-property, cybersecurity, and data-protection obligations remain relevant.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central for negative name certificate; Registro Mercantil Provincial at the Company's registered office for deed registration.

Governing statute

Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010 (Ley de Sociedades de Capital, LSC) Articles 4-4.3 (minimum capital), 19-27 (deed and statutes), 62 (fully paid shares), 78-81 (registered office), 209-222 (administrators' appointment and powers).

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura Pública de Constitución (public incorporation deed) with annexed Estatutos Sociales (articles of association).

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 39 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

Standard SL requires a minimum of EUR 3,000 fully subscribed and paid-up at the time the deed is executed (LSC Art. 62). Under LSC Art. 4.3 (sociedad de formación sucesiva), the SL may be formed with paid-up capital of EUR 1 or more in cash, subject to statutory legal-reserve accumulation, dividend and director-remuneration restrictions. Capital must be deposited in the company-in-formation bank account or paid to the Notary; no state escrow is required.

Funding & unlock path:

Paid-in capital rule: Standard SL requires a minimum of EUR 3,000 fully subscribed and paid-up at the time the deed is executed (LSC Art. 62). Under LSC Art. 4.3 (sociedad de formación sucesiva), the SL may be formed with paid-up capital of EUR 1 or more in cash, subject to statutory legal-reserve accumulation, dividend and director-remuneration restrictions. Capital must be deposited in the company-in-formation bank account or paid to the Notary; no state escrow is required.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT) - Tax portal: sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es

E-government filing portal

A foreign entity seeking to establish an SL or carry out taxable activities in Spain must appoint an in-country fiscal representative and obtain a NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) for non-residents. The procedure involves submitting the official Form 036/037 (Censo de empresarios, profesionales y retenedores), accompanied by notarized constitutional documents, a certificate of residence from the origin tax authority, and proof of the legal representative's identity (passport/NIE). The application is processed at the local AEAT office (Subdirección General de Gestión e Inspección) or through the electronic registry using a digital certificate. Upon approval, the NIF is issued and the entity must subsequently obtain a definitive NIF for the Spanish permanent establishment or the branch, as applicable, and file the corresponding corporate income tax registration.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A foreign entity seeking to establish an SL or carry out taxable activities in Spain must appoint an in-country fiscal representative and obtain a NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) for non-residents. The procedure involves submitting the official Form 036/037 (Censo de empresarios, profesionales y retenedores), accompanied by notarized constitutional documents, a certificate of residence from the origin tax authority, and proof of the legal representative's identity (passport/NIE). The application is processed at the local AEAT office (Subdirección General de Gestión e Inspección) or through the electronic registry using a digital certificate. Upon approval, the NIF is issued and the entity must subsequently obtain a definitive NIF for the Spanish permanent establishment or the branch, as applicable, and file the corresponding corporate income tax registration.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

The default classification for an SL is a fully taxable resident entity, subject to Corporate Income Tax (Impuesto sobre Sociedades) on worldwide income; no check-the-box regime exists. Elections available include fiscal consoolidation under the Spanish group tax regime (Régimen de consolidación fiscal) for groups meeting the 75% ownership and unity of decision rules, and the application of the special tax transparency rules for partnership interests (régimen de transparencia fiscal internacional). Hybrid mismatch election mechanisms are limited to the implemetation of EU ATAD and must be disclosed through tax Form 022 in accordance with DAC6 rules.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general economic turnover threshold applies for VAT registration in Spain; all persons or entities carrying out taxable supplies must register as a taxable person before commencing operations. For intra-EU distance sales from Spain to other Member States, the relevant cross-border threshold is EUR 10,000 (or EUR 3,000 for digital services for temporary B2C distance sales until 2024, now aligned with the EU One Stop Shop threshold).

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Zero-rating is available for the export of goods outside the EU, provided the exporter holds proof of physical shipment and the customs export formalities are completed under Article 21 of the Spanish VAT Law (LEY 37/1992). For services, zero-rating applies when the recipient is established outside the EU or when the service is directly related to the export of tangible goods, provided the service is rendered for business purposes. The supplier must obtain valid documentary evidence of the recipient's status (e.g., TIN number, certificate of establishment) and, if applicable, evidence of the export transport (customs declaration, bill of lading, and commercial invoice). For digital no-code SaaS platforms, zero-rating for intra-EU B2B services applies only when the customer provides a valid VAT number; if no VAT number is supplied, default to Spanish VAT applies.

  • Customs Export Declaration (DEX - Documento Único Administrativo / National Shipment Declaration)
  • Bill of Lading or Airway Bill / Transport Document
  • Commercial Invoice with Incoterms and HS classification
  • Inward Remittance Certificate (justifying receipt of consideration from abroad)
  • Bank SWIFT transfer evidence / proof of payment from non-EU party

Spain mandates B2B electronic invoicing under Law 28/2022 (Crea y Crece) requiring software solutions to maintain invoice integrity, legibility and machine-readability, with standardized data fields. For large companies (turnover > EUR 6,010,121.04) and those applying the VAT group regime, the SII (Suministro Inmediato de Información) is compulsory, requiring near-real-time submission of all invoice records to AEAT via web services (XML over HTTPS with an electronic certificate). Digital stamping or cryptographic seal is not generally required, but AEAT validates and cross-checks the submitted SII records. Smaller taxpayers may opt into voluntary SII. The system does not constitute a fiscal clearance (pre-approval) mechanism but imposes a 4-day time limit for submitting invoice records after issuance/receipt.

Export zero-rating claims are subject to strict documentary review by AEAT. In the event of unjustified zero-rating or failure to produce the statutory documentation, AEAT will assess unrecovered VAT with late interest, impose penalties under Article 171 of the Ley General Tributaria (sanction grade: serious if false documentation; base penalty of 50%-150% of the tax lost), and apply retrospective clawback within the statute of limitations (up to 4 years). Deliberate fraud constituting a criminal offence may attract criminal penalties under Article 305 of the Spanish Penal Code (range: 1-6 years' imprisonment). Additionally, the fraudster's authorization under EU VAT schemes is suspended and the taxpayer is included in the AEAT restrictive registry (Registro de Expedientes de Fraude).

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

The euro is fully convertible for current-account and capital-account transactions. Spain has no general exchange controls, mandatory conversion of foreign-currency receipts, or general restriction on repatriation of dividends, interest, loan principal, or liquidation proceeds. Cross-border payments remain subject to anti-money-laundering, sanctions, tax, transfer-pricing, beneficial-ownership, and foreign-investment reporting requirements. Dividend remittance requires distributable accounting profits, corporate-law approvals, applicable withholding-tax analysis, and compliance with Spanish corporate-law reserve requirements. Interest, royalties, and related-party financing may require withholding, treaty relief documentation, arm's-length support, and transfer-pricing records. Payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions, high-risk countries, opaque ownership, unusual payment chains, or unsupported commercial purposes may be delayed or rejected by the bank.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no statutory export-proceeds surrender requirement, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no general statutory deadline requiring conversion of foreign-currency export receipts into euros. The company may retain export proceeds in foreign-currency accounts, subject to bank onboarding, transaction monitoring, accounting, tax, and financial-reporting controls. Export documentation, invoices, contracts, shipping or service-delivery evidence, and payment records should be retained under applicable Spanish accounting, tax, and anti-money-laundering recordkeeping rules. Goods exports may require customs declarations through the EU customs framework; digital services generally require appropriate invoicing, VAT-location analysis, and evidence of customer location.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España, operating within the framework of the European Central Bank and the European System of Central Banks. Foreign-exchange and capital-movement rules are principally derived from European Union law, Spanish Law 19/2003 on the Legal Regime of Capital Movements and Economic Transactions Abroad, and its implementing regulations.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Stripe Fit: High

Medium for payment collection and operating disbursements; low as a substitute for the principal Spanish corporate bank. An EU-authorised electronic money institution or payment institution may provide payment accounts, safeguarding, card acquiring, international transfers, and certain foreign-exchange services under passporting or local authorisation. It does not provide a Spanish bank deposit unless separately licensed as a credit institution, and safeguarding is not equivalent to deposit protection. The company must verify the provider's authorisation, safeguarding model, eligible countries, settlement currencies, chargeback rules, account-termination rights, beneficial-owner acceptance, and access to SEPA and SWIFT rails. Offshore digital EMIs may refuse Spanish entities, restrict third-party collections, impose transaction limits, or require a European Economic Area nexus. Stripe and Paddle are payment-service and merchant-of-record or billing arrangements, not replacements for a treasury bank account; settlement, reserves, refunds, chargebacks, VAT, and customer-funds flows must be reconciled separately.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Non-resident shareholder or director with incomplete Spanish tax identification, expired identification documents, or inconsistent personal data.

Root cause: Non-resident shareholder or director with incomplete Spanish tax identification, expired identification documents, or inconsistent personal data.

Defense evidence: Valid passport or national identity document; Spanish foreigner identification number where applicable; certified address evidence; tax-residence certificate; notarised or apostilled documents where requested; consistent spelling across corporate, banking, tax, and registry records; signed director and beneficial-owner declarations.
Opaque ownership chain, nominee shareholder, trust, bearer-like arrangement, or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Root cause: Opaque ownership chain, nominee shareholder, trust, bearer-like arrangement, or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Defense evidence: Complete ownership chart to each natural-person beneficial owner; shareholder register; incorporation and constitutional documents for every intermediate entity; certificates of incumbency or good standing; beneficial-owner declaration; corporate resolutions; proof of control rights; trust or foundation documents where relevant.
Insufficient explanation of the no-code website-builder business, expected transaction profile, or use of payment processors.

Root cause: Insufficient explanation of the no-code website-builder business, expected transaction profile, or use of payment processors.

Defense evidence: Business plan; website and product demonstration; customer and supplier profiles; standard contracts and terms of service; pricing and subscription model; Stripe and Paddle agreements; projected monthly volumes; expected countries and currencies; refund and chargeback policy; sample invoices; data-flow and funds-flow diagram.
Inbound shareholder funding that does not match the registered shareholder, approved capital transaction, or stated source of wealth.

Root cause: Inbound shareholder funding that does not match the registered shareholder, approved capital transaction, or stated source of wealth.

Defense evidence: Capital-increase or shareholder-loan agreement; corporate resolution; bank-origin statements; audited or official financial statements of the funding entity; source-of-funds and source-of-wealth memorandum; tax-residence evidence; payment instruction identifying the company and purpose; capital-account certificate where issued.
Payments involving high-risk, sanctioned, restricted, or unexpected jurisdictions, including Latin American counterparties with incomplete information.

Root cause: Payments involving high-risk, sanctioned, restricted, or unexpected jurisdictions, including Latin American counterparties with incomplete information.

Defense evidence: Counterparty KYC file; beneficial-owner screening; sanctions and adverse-media screening; signed commercial contract; invoice; service-delivery or export evidence; reason for jurisdiction selection; transaction-monitoring approval; documented sanctions-screening procedure; escalation record for exceptions.
Large, rapid, circular, third-party, cash-like, or pass-through transactions inconsistent with the company's expected activity.

Root cause: Large, rapid, circular, third-party, cash-like, or pass-through transactions inconsistent with the company's expected activity.

Defense evidence: Rolling cash-flow forecast; transaction-level invoices and contracts; reconciliation between processor reports, bank statements, accounting ledger, and VAT records; explanation of refunds, reserves, intercompany transfers, and shareholder transactions; board approval for exceptional payments; documented treasury policy.
Mismatch between declared business activity and actual payment flows, including marketplace collections, customer-money handling, or regulated financial activity.

Root cause: Mismatch between declared business activity and actual payment flows, including marketplace collections, customer-money handling, or regulated financial activity.

Defense evidence: Legal classification memorandum confirming software and digital-service activities; payment-processing agreements; evidence that customer funds are not held or transferred as an independent regulated service; terms identifying the merchant of record; regulatory perimeter analysis; licences or registrations if the model changes.
Tax-residency, permanent-establishment, VAT, or transfer-pricing concerns arising from cross-border operations.

Root cause: Tax-residency, permanent-establishment, VAT, or transfer-pricing concerns arising from cross-border operations.

Defense evidence: Tax-residence certificates; group structure chart; intercompany agreements; transfer-pricing policy; VAT registrations and filings where applicable; permanent-establishment analysis; employee and contractor location matrix; evidence of service performance and allocation of economic substance.
Failure to maintain current corporate records or inconsistency between the Registro Mercantil, tax authority, bank mandate, and beneficial-owner information.

Root cause: Failure to maintain current corporate records or inconsistency between the Registro Mercantil, tax authority, bank mandate, and beneficial-owner information.

Defense evidence: Recent registry extract; deed of incorporation and amendments; current bylaws; director appointment evidence; shareholder resolutions; bank mandate; Spanish tax identification certificate; beneficial-owner filing or supporting declaration; annual review calendar.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Route paid-in capital through an account held in the Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada's name, preferably from the subscribing shareholder's account or another fully documented account belonging to the same legal person. Use a clear payment reference such as 'share capital contribution' or 'shareholder loan', consistent with the relevant corporate resolution and agreement. Obtain the bank's capital-funding certificate where required for incorporation or capital increase formalities. For a shareholder loan, execute the loan agreement before funding, define maturity, interest, repayment, subordination, and transfer-pricing terms, and assess withholding tax and related-party reporting. Use SEPA Credit Transfer for euro funding where available and SWIFT MT103 or equivalent international wire messaging for non-SEPA currencies. Provide the bank with the purpose, sender, beneficiary, ultimate beneficial owners, source of funds, source of wealth, and supporting corporate documents. Review whether a foreign-investment declaration, statistical reporting, or other notification is required under Spanish foreign-investment rules, particularly for non-EU investors, regulated sectors, or transactions subject to screening. Reconcile the bank credit to the corporate ledger and retain payment confirmation, FX rate, fees, and documentary evidence.Use SEPA Credit Transfer or SEPA Instant where operationally appropriate for euro payments within the SEPA area. Use SWIFT MT103 or the bank's equivalent ISO 20022 cross-border payment message for non-SEPA transfers, with accurate ordering-customer, beneficiary, intermediary-bank, purpose, invoice, and sanctions-screening data. For material software, infrastructure, or supplier purchases, retain the contract, purchase order, invoice, proof of delivery or service performance, and approval evidence. Commercial letters of credit may be issued, advised, confirmed, or discounted through a Spanish bank for qualifying goods transactions; documentary collections may be used where the counterparty and credit risk justify them. Digital-service payments generally use ordinary bank transfers, card settlement, or regulated payment processors rather than documentary trade instruments. Apply dual approval, beneficiary verification, segregation of duties, payment limits, sanctions screening, and three-way reconciliation. Consider withholding tax, VAT, reverse-charge, permanent-establishment, transfer-pricing, and non-deductibility issues before paying foreign suppliers or related parties.Spot foreign-exchange purchases and sales for legitimate operating, investment, or settlement requirements.Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards with an authorised bank, supported by an identified or forecast commercial exposure and documented treasury approval.Foreign-exchange swaps for liquidity and currency-management purposes with an authorised bank.Currency swaps or cross-currency interest-rate swaps for documented financing or long-term currency exposures, subject to bank suitability, collateral, accounting, and documentation requirements.Non-deliverable forwards where the currency, counterparty, and product are legally available and the arrangement is executed through an appropriately authorised financial institution; settlement, reporting, collateral, and regulatory restrictions must be verified before execution.Plain-vanilla currency options or collars for documented commercial exposures where approved by the bank and treasury policy; speculative or disproportionate derivatives activity should be prohibited.All derivative transactions should be covered by appropriate master documentation, exposure records, counterparty limits, valuation controls, confirmation procedures, hedge-accounting analysis where elected, and applicable EMIR reporting or clearing assessments.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium for payment collection and operating disbursements; low as a substitute for the principal Spanish corporate bank. An EU-authorised electronic money institution or payment institution may provide payment accounts, safeguarding, card acquiring, international transfers, and certain foreign-exchange services under passporting or local authorisation. It does not provide a Spanish bank deposit unless separately licensed as a credit institution, and safeguarding is not equivalent to deposit protection. The company must verify the provider's authorisation, safeguarding model, eligible countries, settlement currencies, chargeback rules, account-termination rights, beneficial-owner acceptance, and access to SEPA and SWIFT rails. Offshore digital EMIs may refuse Spanish entities, restrict third-party collections, impose transaction limits, or require a European Economic Area nexus. Stripe and Paddle are payment-service and merchant-of-record or billing arrangements, not replacements for a treasury bank account; settlement, reserves, refunds, chargebacks, VAT, and customer-funds flows must be reconciled separately.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% general Corporate Income Tax rate. Newly incorporated companies may generally apply 15% for the first profitable tax period and the immediately following period, subject to statutory eligibility and anti-abuse conditions. Qualifying micro-enterprises may benefit from reduced rates under applicable transitional legislation.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax generally applies to dividends paid by a Spanish SL to non-residents. The EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive exemption may reduce withholding to 0% where statutory conditions are satisfied, commonly including qualifying EU or EEA parent status, minimum participation, holding-period requirements, subject-to-tax status, beneficial ownership and anti-abuse requirements. A treaty may provide a lower rate, commonly 5%, 10% or 15%, depending on the treaty and ownership level. Spanish-resident corporate recipients may qualify for the domestic participation exemption rather than withholding in qualifying cases.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Modelo 200 is due within the first 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the end of the tax year. For a calendar-year company ending 31 December, the normal deadline is 25 July. If the deadline falls on a non-business day, the deadline moves according to applicable administrative deadline rules. Modelo 202 is generally due during the first 20 calendar days of April, October and December. Modelo 232 is generally due during the month following the ten-month period after the end of the tax year; for a 31 December year-end, the normal deadline is 30 November.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally the first 20 calendar days of April, October and December. Large companies and entities subject to the minimum-payment regime may calculate payments using the current-period accounting base rather than only the prior-year tax liability.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally due during the month following the ten-month period after the end of the tax year. For a 31 December year-end, the normal deadline is 30 November.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Spain does not use one universal monetary threshold for all transfer-pricing documentation. A Local File is generally required for Spanish related-party transactions unless a statutory exemption applies, including the aggregate EUR 250,000 threshold for transactions with the same related person or entity in the same transaction category, subject to exclusions and special rules. A Master File is generally required where the Spanish entity belongs to a group required to prepare it and the group turnover is at least EUR 45 million. The EUR 250,000 threshold does not eliminate the arm's-length requirement, accounting support or the possibility of an AEAT information request. Modelo 232 has separate reporting thresholds, including the EUR 250,000 same-category and same-counterparty threshold and special tests for certain transactions.

Economic substance scope: Spain has no separate UAE-style Economic Substance Regulations regime. Substance is nevertheless material under Spanish anti-abuse rules, the General Anti-Avoidance Rule, the principal-purpose test, beneficial-ownership standards, the EU Parent-Subsidiary and Interest and Royalties Directives, controlled-foreign-company rules, treaty interpretation and the Spanish tax-residence and permanent-establishment rules. The SL should maintain Spanish management capacity, decision-making, personnel or outsourced operational control, premises where commercially appropriate, software-development and customer-support evidence, bank and accounting controls, and genuine commercial reasons for intercompany arrangements. A mailbox company, pass-through royalty or financing vehicle, circular funds flow, or unsupported management-fee arrangement may be denied treaty or directive benefits and recharacterized.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate Income Tax Evasion

Statutory sanction: Administrative tax penalties may range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax depending on concealment, repeated conduct and fraud indicators. Tax fraud exceeding EUR 120,000 per tax period may constitute a criminal offense, generally punishable by imprisonment of 1 to 5 years and a fine of 1 to 6 times the amount defrauded, together with possible loss of public subsidies and contracting rights. Aggravated cases, including amounts exceeding EUR 600,000 or organized conduct, may attract imprisonment of 2 to 6 years and higher ancillary sanctions.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers may incur criminal liability where they personally participate, authorize or knowingly facilitate the fraud. Civil tax liability may extend to administrators who negligently or intentionally fail to ensure compliance. Travel bans, asset freezing and other restrictions require judicial or enforcement orders; they are not automatic.
False Invoicing and VAT Fraud

Statutory sanction: VAT assessments, repayment of improperly claimed credits, late-payment interest and administrative penalties may apply. Serious VAT fraud can result in penalties of 50% to 100% or more of the improperly reduced or refunded amount, subject to statutory classification. Criminal tax fraud may apply where the tax threshold and intent requirements are met.

Director personal liability: Directors may face subsidiary liability for unpaid tax and criminal liability for knowing participation. Courts may impose asset measures or travel restrictions during criminal proceedings; imprisonment is possible only where criminal elements are established.
Transfer-Pricing Non-Compliance

Statutory sanction: Specific documentation penalties may generally equal 1% of omitted or inaccurately stated transactions, subject to statutory minimums and maximums, and tax adjustment penalties may generally equal 15% of the resulting adjustment or the applicable statutory percentage. Additional tax, interest and general penalties may apply.

Director personal liability: The SL remains primarily liable. Directors may incur subsidiary tax liability for willful or negligent failure to comply and criminal liability where transfer-pricing manipulation forms part of intentional tax fraud.
Improper Dividend or Profit Repatriation

Statutory sanction: The company may owe withholding tax, late-payment interest, surcharges and penalties. Invalid distributions may require restitution to the company and may create shareholder repayment liability under Spanish corporate law. Directors may be liable for damage caused by unlawful distributions.

Director personal liability: Directors can face civil restitution and damages claims, and potentially criminal liability for insolvency, accounting fraud or tax evasion. Travel bans or imprisonment require judicial proceedings and are not automatic consequences of an incorrect dividend.
Shell Company and Artificial Substance

Statutory sanction: AEAT may deny treaty, participation-exemption or directive benefits, recharacterize transactions, assess tax and interest, impose penalties and apply anti-abuse provisions. Sham transactions may be treated as nonexistent for tax purposes and may support criminal tax-fraud charges where thresholds and intent are met.

Director personal liability: Directors and beneficial owners may face civil, tax and criminal liability for deliberate artificiality. Courts may order asset preservation, director disqualification or travel restrictions where legally justified.
Anti-Money Laundering and Beneficial-Ownership Failures

Statutory sanction: Under Spanish Law 10/2010, serious and very serious breaches may attract significant administrative fines, potentially up to EUR 10 million or 10% of annual turnover for certain very serious breaches, together with public reprimand, temporary or permanent disqualification and authorization consequences. Criminal money laundering may carry imprisonment, fines and confiscation.

Director personal liability: Compliance officers, directors and beneficial owners may be personally sanctioned or prosecuted where they participate in or knowingly permit the conduct. Asset freezing, travel restrictions and imprisonment require the applicable administrative or judicial process.
Accounting, Corporate-Books and Annual-Accounts Failure

Statutory sanction: The Commercial Registry may close the company's register, and corporate and administrative penalties may apply. False accounting, insolvency concealment or use of fabricated accounts may constitute criminal offenses with fines or imprisonment depending on the conduct.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur civil liability for creditor and shareholder losses, insolvency-related liability and criminal liability for intentional false accounting. Disqualification from managing companies may follow insolvency or criminal proceedings.
Unlawful Insolvency and Asset Diversion

Statutory sanction: Transactions may be rescinded, assets recovered and directors disqualified. Insolvency-related criminal offenses can carry imprisonment and fines where concealment, asset stripping or creditor prejudice is proven.

Director personal liability: Directors may be ordered to cover all or part of the insolvency deficit, repay diverted assets and compensate creditors. Judicial asset measures, travel restrictions and imprisonment may apply only through the relevant proceedings.
Digital Services, IP and Permanent Establishment Mischaracterization

Statutory sanction: AEAT may assert Spanish taxable income, permanent-establishment profit, withholding obligations, VAT obligations, interest and penalties. Repeated or intentional concealment may escalate into criminal tax exposure.

Director personal liability: Directors may be personally liable for negligent tax governance and criminally liable for deliberate concealment. Contractual outsourcing does not eliminate liability where the SL controls the relevant functions or knowingly misstates the operating model.
Payment-Processor and Platform Reconciliation Failure

Statutory sanction: Unreported revenue may generate Corporate Income Tax and VAT assessments, interest, surcharges and penalties. Data obtained through EU and international exchange mechanisms may support a discovery assessment and fraud investigation.

Director personal liability: Directors may face subsidiary tax liability and criminal exposure if omissions are deliberate or materially fraudulent. Personal sanctions depend on participation, knowledge and statutory thresholds.
